desc:
A grid is a board where 0 marks a free square and 1 a blocked square. A chess queen stands on the free square (sr, sc). In one move the queen slides any number (at least one) of squares in one of the 8 directions (along a row, a column or a diagonal). Every square it passes over and the square where it stops must be free; it cannot jump over or land on a blocked square.

Return the minimum number of moves to bring the queen to the free square (tr, tc), or -1 if that is impossible. If the two squares are equal the answer is 0.

grid = [[0,0,0],
        [0,1,0],
        [0,0,0]],  start = (0,0), target = (2,2)

result = 2     ((0,0) -> (0,2) -> (2,2))
constraints: The start and the target squares are free (0) and inside the board
hints: Each queen move is one edge, no matter how far the queen slides. Squares are nodes, so BFS counts moves.
From a square, walk in each of the 8 directions step by step, stopping at the board edge or a blocked square; every free square on the way is a neighbour at distance +1.

To keep the sliding cheap, stop a ray when you meet a square whose distance is already smaller than or equal to the current one: that square will itself cover the rest of the ray. Squares at exactly distance + 1 may be passed through.
editorial: The moves of a sliding piece form an unweighted graph whose edges are 'can reach by one slide', so BFS over squares gives the minimum number of moves. The neighbours of a square are all free squares you meet while walking outward in each direction until a wall or the border.

Naive expansion costs O(max(R,C)) per direction per square, which is still fine for a 40 × 40 board (about 40 · 40 · 8 · 40 steps). A standard pruning makes it linear in practice: while sliding from a square with distance d, if you meet a square with distance ≤ d, stop, because that square (and the ones beyond it) was or will be expanded with an equal or better distance; if the square is unvisited, label it d + 1; if it already has d + 1, keep walking.
Return the distance when the target is dequeued; if the queue runs out, the answer is -1. Note that on an open board the answer is at most 2, so interesting cases come from walls that cut rays.
